My Lord, I speak to you, as a citizen of the United States, and as a member of one of its noblest bodies, the Supreme Court of the Union, when the country has called upon it to defend one of those institutions for which it is most earnestly contended. It has never been the habit of the Court to resist such calls. When the Government of the country has demanded its aid, in behalf of the public peace, the Court has, from time to time, given the Government some form of help; and, when the country has appealed to it in the cause of liberty, it has, at all times, rendered what assistance it could. And now, when a part of the American people has thought fit to call upon it for support, in the defense of one of the great pillars of our political system, the Court has undertaken the work with its usual readiness.

In the case before us the Court is requested to declare that the laws made in pursuance of the Constitution of the United States do not deprive one of its citizens of his freedom of speech and of his freedom of press. That is the only question we have to decide. We have no right to say more.

samples.prompt: Write three short anecdotal examples illustrating how unconventional or eccentric behavior can be more persuasive than eloquent rhetoric.
samples.generated:
Once a gentleman of some pretensions in his own opinion, but withal a most absurd person, went to a dinner-party, and took off his hat as he entered the room; so that the company were much astonished to see him do it. "Why," said he, "I take it off to show my respect to the house." But this made them still more surprised. He was asked what house he meant? "The one above me," says he. "But you cannot take off your hat to every house you meet with," replied they. "Then I will take off mine to the next house below me," said he; and then took off his hat again. This is the way with such people; if they speak well, they talk well too. ["_The Spectator_"]

A young man, in whose conversation it was a pleasure to hear anything, and who had a great deal to say, when he pleased, met a very good-looking lady at a ball. samples.real:
We have read of some celebrated philosopher who was so absent-minded
that he paid a call at his own house. My own absent-mindedness is
extreme, and my philosophy, of course, is the marvel of men and angels.
But I never quite managed to be so absent-minded as that. Some yards at
least from my own door, something vaguely familiar has always caught
my eye; and thus the joke has been spoiled. Of course I have quite
constantly walked into another man's house, thinking it was my own
house; my visits became almost monotonous. But walking into my own house
and thinking it was another man's house is a flight of poetic detachment
still beyond me. Something of the sensations that such an absent-minded
man must feel I really felt the other day; and very pleasant sensations
they were. The best parts of every proper romance are the first chapter
and the last chapter; and to knock at a strange door and find a nice
wife would be to concentrate the beginning and end of all romance.

same kind. For I strolled through a place I had imagined quite virgin
